newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RGC sees Sierra Rutile reopening.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RGC sees Sierra Rutile reopening.

text.p: Australian mining group RGC Ltd said on Wednesday it was confident the closed Sierra Rutile Co mine in Sierra Leone can be reopened but said the political situation in the West African nation remained unstable.
RGC group general manager mineral sands Keith Faulkner, who spend a week in the country earlier this month, said the visit verified previous estimates of damage at about A$25 million.
"The major items of equipment aren't severely damaged," he told Reuters after RGC's annual general meeting.
RGC acquired its indirect stake in the mine after acquiring 77 percent of Cudgen RZ Ltd earlier this year.
Cudgen in turn owns 50.1 percent of Consolidated Rutile Ltd, which has a half-share in Sierra Rutile with U.S.-based Nord Resources Corp.
Faulkner said if a suitable level of security could be achieved in the next six months, rehabilitation of the mine could begin in July 1997 and production in January 1998.
"If the government can secure a peace agreement in the next six months, then I think that timeframe is achieveable," he said.
However, Faulkner said the political situation remained unstable, and noted that a previous timetable would have seen production start this quarter.
The present government appeared to have the support of the international community, but had not yet signed a peace deal with rebel forces who overran the mine in January 1995, he said.
Sierra Rutile had told the government it could not restart the operation without security for employees, both expatriate and local, and security for assets.
Faulkner said the mine could be restarted for A$25 million, but in total an A$80 million refinancing plan would be needed to rehabilitate the mine and complete an expansion plan.
The Sierra Leone mine produced 144,000 tonnes of rutile in the year to June 1994, a quarter of the world total at the time.
Faulkner said he was aware of concerns RGC might not want the mine restarted given the likely effect on rutile prices.
"As a competitor it was certainly better for us to see it out of the market place, but as part of our business we are quite happy to see it in operation," he said.
